questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer from Bihar presents with a single hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on his forearm and thickening of the ulnar nerve. Slit-skin smear shows no bacilli. Biopsy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells but no AFB. Which type of leprosy does this patient have?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) features a single well-defined anaesthetic patch, thickened peripheral nerve, negative slit-skin smear (paucibacillary), and well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells but no AFB. Strong cell-mediated immunity controls bacterial replication. BT shows 2–5 patches with less well-defined granulomas.

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on an urticarial erythematous base over the trunk and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. Salt-split skin shows staining on the epidermal (roof) side. Which antigen is the primary target?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid targets BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230 within hemidesmosomes. Staining on the epidermal roof of salt-split skin distinguishes it from EBA (dermal floor staining). Tense subepidermal bullae on urticarial base in elderly is the classic presentation. Desmoglein 1 and 3 are targeted in pemphigus (intraepidermal). Type VII collagen is targeted in EBA.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man has a 2.5 mm Breslow thickness melanoma on his back with no ulceration and no clinical or radiological evidence of nodal or distant metastasis. According to AJCC 8th edition staging, what is the correct T category?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition melanoma T staging: T3 = Breslow thickness 2.01–4.0 mm. Suffix 'a' = no ulceration, 'b' = ulceration present. A 2.5 mm non-ulcerated melanoma = T3a. T2 covers 1.01–2.0 mm; T4 covers >4.0 mm. Ulceration upgrades the T suffix and worsens prognosis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with painful erosions on the oral mucosa and flaccid bullae on the trunk that rupture easily leaving raw areas. Nikolsky's sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposition in a 'chicken wire' pattern throughout the epidermis. Which protein is the primary target?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris primarily targets desmoglein 3 (mucosal dominant) and both Dsg3 and Dsg1 (mucocutaneous type). The 'chicken wire' or 'fish-net' DIF pattern reflects intercellular IgG throughout the epidermis. Flaccid blisters are due to loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis). Desmoglein 1 is the target in pemphigus foliaceus (no mucosal involvement).

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis 3 weeks after unprotected sex. Regional lymph nodes are rubbery and non-tender. VDRL is non-reactive but TPHA is positive. What is the correct interpretation?
opts: Primary syphilis — treponemal tests (TPHA) become positive before non-treponemal tests (VDRL)
Secondary syphilis — VDRL is always reactive in the secondary stage
Latent syphilis — both tests should be reactive
Biological false positive — TPHA result should be ignored
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, specific treponemal tests (TPHA, FTA-ABS) seroconvert earlier than non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR). VDRL may still be negative in early primary syphilis. A painless indurated chancre with rubbery non-tender lymphadenopathy appearing ~3 weeks after exposure is classic primary syphilis. TPHA positivity confirms treponemal infection.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child has scaling patches on the scalp with hair loss and fluorescence under Wood's lamp. KOH mount shows arthroconidia arranged outside and around the hair shaft (ectothrix). Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes ectothrix tinea capitis with bright yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's lamp (due to pteridine production). T. tonsurans and T. violaceum cause endothrix infections (arthroconidia inside hair) with no Wood's lamp fluorescence. Epidermophyton floccosum infects skin and nails but never hair.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis unresponsive to methotrexate and cyclosporine is started on a biologic that selectively inhibits IL-17A. PASI drops from 28 to 2 after 16 weeks. Which drug best fits this description?
questions.exp: Secukinumab and ixekizumab are monoclonal antibodies that selectively bind and neutralise IL-17A, a key cytokine in psoriasis pathogenesis. They achieve PASI 90 responses in ~60–70% of patients. Ustekinumab targets the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23. Risankizumab and guselkumab target the p19 subunit of IL-23 specifically.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops widespread targetoid lesions, erosions of oral mucosa and conjunctivae, and epidermal detachment of 35% BSA after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 14 days ago. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: IVIG 1 g/kg/day for 3 days plus drug withdrawal
Immediate drug withdrawal and transfer to a burns unit for supportive care
questions.exp: Epidermal detachment >30% BSA = TEN (Lyell syndrome). Cornerstone of management is immediate withdrawal of the causative drug and supportive care in a burns/ICU setting (IV fluids, wound care, nutrition, ophthalmology review). Evidence for IVIG and cyclosporine is debated; systemic corticosteroids are generally contraindicated due to increased infection risk and impaired wound healing.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman has butterfly rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthralgia, and positive ANA (1:640, homogeneous). Which antibody, if positive, is MOST specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Smith (Sm) has the highest specificity (~99%) for SLE, although sensitivity is only 25–30%. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific and correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro is associated with Sjogren's syndrome and neonatal lupus. Anti-histone is the hallmark of drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid).

questions.q: A 42-year-old man has intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. Which associated systemic condition must be screened for?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) shows granular IgA at DEJ and is strongly associated with celiac disease in >90% of cases. Anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG IgA) and anti-endomysial antibodies are elevated. A gluten-free diet treats both the gut and skin; dapsone controls itch but not the underlying enteropathy.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man has generalised erythroderma, severe pruritus, and lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood shows large lymphocytes with convoluted 'cerebriform' nuclei >1000/mm³. Flow cytometry reveals CD4+CD8- T-cell phenotype. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sezary syndrome is the leukaemic/erythrodermic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: triad of erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sezary cells (>1000 CD4+ cerebriform T-cells/mm³). It differs from erythrodermic mycosis fungoides by significant blood involvement. HTLV-1-associated adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma has hypercalcaemia and lytic bone lesions.

questions.q: A 17-year-old girl has comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodulo-cystic lesions on the face and back causing scarring, unresponsive to topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, and two courses of oral doxycycline. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Switch to oral minocycline plus topical clindamycin
Intralesional triamcinolone for individual lesions only
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin is the treatment of choice for severe nodulocystic acne, scarring acne, or acne unresponsive to two adequate antibiotic courses. It targets all four pathogenic factors of acne: sebum production, follicular keratinisation, P. acnes colonisation, and inflammation. A cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg is the therapeutic target.

questions.q: An 8-year-old boy and his mother both present with nocturnal pruritus. Linear burrows in the finger web spaces and axillae are seen. KOH of burrow scrapings confirms the diagnosis. What is the correct first-line treatment and application method?
opts: Permethrin 5% cream — apply from neck down, leave 8–14 hours, repeat after 1 week
Lindane 1% lotion — apply all over body including scalp, wash off after 6 hours
Benzyl benzoate 25% — apply from neck down, wash off after 1 hour
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg single dose — no topical treatment needed
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is first-line for scabies. Applied from neck down (including scalp and face in infants), left for 8–14 hours overnight, then washed off. Repeated after 1 week. All household contacts treated simultaneously. Lindane is contraindicated in children and pregnant women due to neurotoxicity. Oral ivermectin is preferred for crusted scabies or mass treatment.

questions.q: A 6-year-old immunocompetent child has multiple pearly, umbilicated, dome-shaped papules on the trunk. The mother asks about treatment. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 7 days
Watchful waiting — lesions self-resolve in 6–18 months
Topical imiquimod 5% cream three times weekly
Liquid nitrogen cryotherapy to each lesion
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum in immunocompetent children is self-limiting; lesions resolve spontaneously in 6–18 months (occasionally up to 2 years). Watchful waiting avoids painful and traumatic procedures in young children. Active treatment (cantharidin, curettage, cryotherapy) is reserved for widespread or cosmetically distressing disease. Acyclovir is ineffective as MC is a poxvirus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old alcoholic man has blisters on sun-exposed skin (dorsa of hands), skin fragility, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Urine shows pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) results from deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD), causing accumulation of uroporphyrins that are excreted in urine and cause photosensitivity. It is the most common porphyria. Precipitants include alcohol, iron overload, HCV, oestrogen. Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP). PBGD deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria (no skin lesions).

questions.q: A 22-year-old man has multiple hypopigmented macules on the trunk that fail to tan. Wood's lamp shows pale yellowish fluorescence. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the recommended topical treatment?
opts: Clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for 4 weeks
Selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion applied for 10 min daily for 1 week
Ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied to skin, rinsed after 5 minutes daily for 3 days
Terbinafine 1% cream twice daily for 2 weeks
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. 'Spaghetti and meatballs' (short hyphae and round spores) on KOH is pathognomonic. Ketoconazole 2% shampoo applied to skin and rinsed after 5 minutes for 3 consecutive days is a widely used convenient topical regimen. Selenium sulfide is also effective. Terbinafine has poor activity against Malassezia due to its mechanism of action not affecting this organism's sterol pathways effectively.

questions.q: A 26-year-old man has a painless genital ulcer followed by unilateral matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. Examination shows the 'groove sign' (Poupart's ligament divides the swollen lymph nodes). Aspirate shows Gram-negative intracellular organisms. Treatment of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. Classic presentation: transient painless ulcer → painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with groove sign (pathognomonic when present). Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days (WHO/CDC recommendation). Azithromycin 1 g is used for uncomplicated chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis, not LGV.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man develops a firm raised scar that extends beyond the original wound margins on the chest after surgery, continuing to grow 18 months later. Intralesional triamcinolone injections are given. What is the most effective adjunct to steroid injections for keloids?
questions.exp: Keloids extend beyond wound margins and continue growing. First-line treatment is intralesional corticosteroids (triamcinolone 10–40 mg/mL) combined with silicone gel sheeting. Silicone sheets reduce TGF-β, decrease fibroblast activity, and improve hydration — flattening scars over months. Surgical excision alone has >50% recurrence for keloids; excision must be combined with post-operative corticosteroids or radiation.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman has chalk-white depigmented patches on her face and dorsa of hands. Wood's lamp shows bright white fluorescence. Which dermoscopy finding best predicts repigmentation potential?
opts: Diffuse white glow throughout the patch
Perifollicular pigmentation within the depigmented patch
questions.exp: Perifollicular pigmentation on dermoscopy indicates residual melanocytes in follicular reservoirs within the patch, which serve as a source for repigmentation. It is a positive prognostic sign and helps guide treatment decisions (e.g., phototherapy is more likely to succeed). Perifollicular repigmentation is the earliest sign of response to therapy in vitiligo.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has flat-topped, violaceous polygonal papules on flexor wrists and Wickham's striae on buccal mucosa. Biopsy shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ with colloid (civatte) bodies. What is the underlying pathomechanism?
opts: Type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE and mast cells
Type IV hypersensitivity — CD8+ T-cell-mediated cytotoxicity against basal keratinocytes
Type II hypersensitivity — IgG autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes
Neutrophil-mediated destruction of the dermoepidermal junction
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated lichenoid interface dermatitis. CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes accumulate at the DEJ and destroy basal keratinocytes presenting altered/unknown antigens, causing vacuolar degeneration and apoptosis (civatte/colloid bodies). Classic 5 Ps: Pruritic, Planar, Polygonal, Purple, Papules. Wickham's striae result from focal thickening of the granular layer.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man on carbamazepine develops SJS/TEN with 15% BSA detachment. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in South Asian populations?
questions.exp: HLA-B*58:01 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in Han Chinese and South/Southeast Asian populations (odds ratio >1000). HLA-B*57:01 is the marker for abacavir hypersensitivity in HIV patients. HLA-A*31:01 is associated with carbamazepine-induced DRESS/SJS in European and Japanese populations. Pre-prescription HLA-B*58:01 screening is recommended in South Asian patients before carbamazepine initiation.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman recurrently develops classic targetoid lesions (three-zone: central dusky area, pale oedematous ring, outer red halo) on palms 5 days after oral herpes outbreaks. No mucosal involvement. Best long-term management is:
opts: Oral prednisolone 40 mg during each episode
Prophylactic oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily
Episodic acyclovir 200 mg five times daily only during active herpes
questions.exp: Herpes-associated recurrent erythema multiforme (HAEM) is triggered by HSV reactivation 1–3 weeks prior to each episode. Long-term suppressive antiviral therapy (acyclovir 400 mg BD or valacyclovir 500 mg BD for 6–12 months) prevents HSV reactivation and thereby prevents EM recurrences. Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in HAEM as they may worsen HSV infection.

questions.q: A 68-year-old fair-skinned farmer presents with a pearly, telangiectatic nodule with a rolled border and central ulceration on the nasolabial fold. What is the most common histological subtype of basal cell carcinoma?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC accounts for 60–80% of all BCCs. It presents as a pearly papule/nodule with rolled borders, surface telangiectasia, and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer') on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Morphoeic BCC (scar-like, ill-defined) has the highest recurrence rate due to subclinical tumour extension. Superficial BCC is flat, erythematous, and more common on the trunk.

questions.q: A newborn presents at birth with tense bullae at trauma sites. Electron microscopy shows cleavage within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Direct immunofluorescence is negative. The baby has widespread bullae and nail dystrophy. Which type of epidermolysis bullosa is this?
questions.exp: Junctional EB results from mutations in laminin-332 (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2) or integrins (ITGA6, ITGB4), causing cleavage within the lamina lucida. Herlitz type is lethal in infancy due to laryngeal and gastrointestinal involvement. EB simplex is intraepidermal (keratin 5/14 mutations). Dystrophic EB is sublamina densa (type VII collagen / COL7A1 mutations). DIF is negative (no autoantibodies).

questions.q: A 30-year-old nurse develops vesicular erythematous dermatitis on her hands after switching to a new brand of latex gloves. Patch testing at 48–96 hours is positive to thiuram mix. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
opts: Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity — allergic contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis — not a true immunological reaction
questions.exp: Positive patch test at 48–96 hours = Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity, mediated by sensitised T-lymphocytes. Rubber accelerators (thiurams, carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazoles) in latex gloves are common contact allergens. True latex allergy (Type I, IgE-mediated) presents with immediate urticaria/anaphylaxis and is diagnosed by skin prick test or serum latex-specific IgE, not patch test.

questions.q: A 26-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 = 120 cells/mm³) has multiple large cauliflower-like perianal and penile warts unresponsive to topical podophyllin for 3 months. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Imiquimod 5% cream three times weekly for up to 16 weeks
High-resolution anoscopy and referral for electrocautery/CO2 laser ablation
Initiate HAART — immune reconstitution will clear the warts
questions.exp: In immunocompromised patients with large-volume, treatment-resistant condylomata acuminata, ablative physical methods (electrocautery, CO2 laser, cryotherapy) are preferred. High-resolution anoscopy (HRA) is mandatory in HIV+ patients with perianal warts to exclude anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN) and anal squamous cell carcinoma — HPV 16/18 carries high oncogenic risk. HAART improves immunity but does not reliably eliminate established warts.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child has dry scaly skin from birth, flexural lichenification in antecubital and popliteal fossae, and intense pruritus. Mother has asthma; father has allergic rhinitis. Serum IgE is elevated. Which of the following is NOT a major diagnostic criterion in Hanifin and Rajka criteria for atopic dermatitis?
opts: Personal or family history of atopy
questions.exp: Hanifin and Rajka major criteria: (1) Pruritus, (2) Typical morphology and distribution (flexural lichenification in adults; facial/extensor in infants), (3) Chronic or chronically relapsing course, (4) Personal or family history of atopy. Elevated serum IgE is a minor criterion. Remember: 3 or more major criteria needed for diagnosis, supported by minor criteria.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules on knuckles, proximal muscle weakness, and elevated CK. Anti-Jo-1 antibody is positive. What does anti-Jo-1 positivity predict in dermatomyositis?
opts: High risk of interstitial lung disease and antisynthetase syndrome
Higher risk of occult internal malignancy
Mild disease with excellent response to steroids alone
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) defines antisynthetase syndrome: myositis + interstitial lung disease (ILD) + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's phenomenon + non-erosive arthritis + fever. ILD occurs in 70–80% of anti-Jo-1-positive patients and is the primary cause of morbidity/mortality. Malignancy risk is highest with anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 antibodies.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with a painful, soft, non-indurated genital ulcer with undermined irregular edges. Unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) is present. Gram stain of ulcer discharge shows Gram-negative rods in 'school of fish' pattern. Treatment of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Characteristic features: painful soft ulcer with undermined edges, unilateral tender bubo, 'school of fish/railway track' pattern on Gram stain. WHO-recommended treatments: Azithromycin 1 g single dose OR Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose OR Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3 days OR Erythromycin 500 mg QID × 7 days. Azithromycin is preferred for single-dose compliance.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer with chronic sun exposure has a firm keratotic ulcerating nodule on the lower lip growing for 4 months. Biopsy confirms well-differentiated SCC. Which single feature most strongly predicts metastatic potential in cutaneous SCC?
opts: Arising on a background of actinic keratosis
questions.exp: Cutaneous SCC high-risk features for metastasis include: diameter >2 cm (raises risk from ~2% to ~30%), thickness >2 mm/Clark level IV–V, poor differentiation, perineural/lymphovascular invasion, immunosuppression, location on lip/ear/non-sun-exposed sites, and recurrent lesions. SCC of the lip has a 10–15% metastatic rate. Well-differentiated histology and sun-exposed location are actually lower-risk features.
